segments.text: Listening Part B. In this part of the test, you'll hear six different extracts. In each extract, you'll hear people talking in a different healthcare setting.
For questions 13 to 19, choose the answer A, B or C, which fits best according to what you hear.
You'll have time to read each question before you listen. Complete your answers as you listen.
Now look at question 13.
You hear two nurses discussing their work attire.
Now read the question.
I really can't believe they make us wear these awful scrubs.
I miss our old uniforms.
What could you possibly miss?
Well, these are hardly flattering.
It's like wearing a sheet.
But the uniforms were uncomfortable and always ended up dirty by the end of the day.
We had to wear them home and wash them.
Worst of all, we needed to iron them.
But scrubs are starchy and they just hang.
Uniforms look so much more professional.
I think we look more like medical professionals when we're all wearing the same thing.
In scrubs, there's no mistaking that we're clinical staff.
Besides, there's far less chance of taking home contaminated clothing.
I'll give you that, sure, but I still think a uniform with a collared shirt presents a more formal image.
Question 14. You hear a podiatrist giving advice to a patient about her Achilles tendonitis.
Now read the question.
The most common causes of Achilles tendonitis are either flimsy shoes that don't provide support when you're running,
or the type of running itself, and of course, duration.
Oh, right. Interesting.
Yeah, the fact that you jog on the beach is certainly a fact that we need to look at,
especially if you don't want this occurring time and time again.
Right. I actually live right opposite the beach, and it's such a relaxing way to exercise.
I'd prefer to keep it up if it's possible.
Oh, it still is. But there are ways to keep your feet healthy at the same time.
Barefoot jogging on sand is generally fine, as the impact isn't so great when it's dry and powdery.
But if it's wet and compacted, you'll need to wear some proper fitting shoes.
The pair that you're currently wearing are appropriate for this.
Great!
You just need that strong support, especially around the ankles, which they provide.
Question 15.
You hear a radiographer briefing a patient about the importance of remaining still during a procedure.
Now read the question.
I'll ask you now to lie on the table of the scanner with your arm positioned above your head like I showed you earlier.
Yeah, sure. It's a little painful when I move it. Would you mind giving me a hand?
Of course. Now remember to try your best to refrain from moving while the scan's in progress.
This is essential for us to achieve a clear picture.
Any movement could blur and distort the image.
That's no problem. But I might doze off. I'm so tired.
It's rather noisy in there, with a lot of clicks and loud bangs, so it's unlikely that will happen.
Oh, that's good news. I'd like to avoid any chance of my arm falling asleep.
Is that something that happens often?
It happens quite regularly when I'm stationary. It doesn't tend to hurt, but the abrupt loss of any sensation is really disconcerting.
It must be. Look, if it happens, make sure to tell us.
OK.
Question 16. You hear a ward manager reminding a group of nursing assistants of their role and responsibility.
Now read the question.
I'll now read to you part of the nursing assistant policy as I wish to make clear what's expected of you here at this hospital.
The role of the nursing assistant encompasses providing help with care, comfort and support
of patients in their activities of daily living and in observing and verbally reporting changes
in patient behaviour. The registered nurse is responsible for delegating appropriately to the
nursing assistant within the limits of his or her knowledge, skill, education and experience.
Delegation of care is based on the characteristics of the patient
and on the complexity of the care required.
At all times, the nursing assistant retains responsibility for their own actions
and remains accountable to the registered nurse for all delegated functions.
Question 17.
You hear a registered nurse providing a handover of a patient's progress.
Now read the question.
Next we have Mr. Floyd, 68 years old.
He presented at 3 a.m. feeling unwell with a rapid onset of shortness of breath.
His SATs were 90%, heart rate 112, and he was efebrile.
Bloods were normal apart from a slightly elevated white cell count.
His original mobile chest x-ray was patchy,
and another has been arranged at the radiography department for 9 a.m.,
so an orderly needs to be called for transfer 15 minutes prior.
ECG showed sinus tachycardia.
No significant history, but as he's recently returned from a long-drive interstate,
therapeutic clexine was started for a possible pulmonary embolism.
His SATs are now 96% on 2 liters of oxygen, but since admission has developed a cough,
right-sided pleuritic chest pain, and fever which is consistent with pneumonia.
So, the doctors ordered a repeat of his bloods, and that he'd be on prophylactic clexine
as well as started on antibiotics as per guidelines.
Question 18.
You hear a consultant discussing the history of a patient's injured shoulder.
Now read the question.
Your MRI shows a minor labral tear of the right shoulder. Can you tell me more about
the injury?
I was playing tennis with my daughter. I used to play semi-professionally, so I was
hoping she might follow in my footsteps. I've been playing for over 30 years, so I figured
I'd coach her myself. She has some real promise. I guess I didn't warm up enough. I forget
sometimes that I'm 50. Anyway, two sets in, my shoulder just felt like it popped.
can definitely be a factor in a torn lab room. In fact, it's one of the more common causes.
You've certainly been playing for a long time now. And as you mentioned, warming up is crucial,
especially as we age. Considering your sporting history, repetitive motion is more likely to be
the culprit, especially at your level of fitness. I see.
